title: Private Service Edge platforms, host OS maintenance, capacity and limits

prose.text: Planning a Private Service Edge deployment is a question of platform, host maintenance, capacity and limits.

supported-platforms.statement: Zscaler distributes Private Service Edge images for enterprise data centers and local private cloud environments such as VMware, and the platforms listed as supported by Private Access are AWS, Docker, GCP, Linux, Microsoft Azure and VMware platforms.

quotes: Zscaler distributes images for deployment in enterprise data centers and local private cloud environments such as VMware.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) - Docker - Google Cloud Platform (GCP) - Linux - Microsoft Azure - VMware Platforms

stig-images.statement: Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) images are available for AWS, GCP, Microsoft Azure and VMware by default.

quotes: Private Access provides Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) images are available for AWS, GCP, Microsoft Azure, and VMware by default.

host-os-enterprise-linux.statement: The console shows each Private Service Edge's run-time OS (for example Enterprise Linux 9) and the compile-time package OS on which its RPM binary is packaged (for example Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9).

quotes: The run time OS on which the Private Service Edge is running (e.g., Enterprise Linux 9).
The compile time OS on which the RPM binary is packaged (e.g., Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9).

throughput-sizing.statement: Each Private Service Edge supports up to 500 Mbps aggregate (inbound plus outbound) throughput, so a 1 Gbps connection needs 2 to 3 Private Service Edges; throughput varies with double encryption, AppProtection and ZDX.

quotes: Each Private Service Edge supports up to 500 Mbps of throughput.
you would need to deploy 2 to 3 Private Service Edges to support the 1 Gbps connection.
whether you have double encryption, AppProtection, or ZDX enabled.
Throughput numbers are aggregate (i.e., total inbound and outbound).
The exact throughput can vary and depends on other network factors such as your internal network setup, latency, and whether you have double encryption, AppProtection, or ZDX enabled.

sizing-table.statement: For up to 500 Mbps per Private Service Edge: up to 2,000 active users need 8 GB RAM (10 GB with ZDX) and 4 vCPUs; up to 4,000 need 16 GB (18 GB) and 8 vCPUs; up to 10,000 need 32 GB (34 GB) and 16 vCPUs; disk is 64 GB thin provisioned and at least 1 NIC.

quotes: | Up to 2,000 | 8 GB (10 GB with ZDX) | 4 vCPUs or 4 CPUs |
| Up to 4,000 | 16 GB (18 GB with ZDX) | 8 vCPUs or 8 CPUs |
| Up to 10,000 | 32 GB (34 GB with ZDX) | 16 vCPUs or 16 CPUs |
Disk Space: 64 GB (thin provisioned) for all deployment platforms
Network Card: 1 NIC (minimum)
The following specifications are recommended by Zscaler for up to 500 Mbps throughput for each Private Service Edge.
| Active Users | Memory | vCPU or CPU Cores |

scale-out-small.statement: Zscaler recommends more Private Service Edges with lower specifications over fewer with higher specifications, because a failure of a large one affects more traffic; they scale elastically within a group.

quotes: Zscaler recommends that you have more Private Service Edges with lower specifications rather than fewer Private Service Edges with higher specifications.
Private Service Edges are designed to scale elastically.

For example, if you have fewer Private Service Edges with higher specifications and one fails, you could adversely affect more user application traffic or sessions than a smaller Private Service Edge that fails.
You can deploy additional Private Service Edges in the same Private Service Edge group to increase the total throughput as required by your deployment.

pairs-n-plus-one.statement: Zscaler recommends deploying Private Service Edges in pairs (N+1), where N is the number needed by the sizing requirements, to keep availability during software upgrades.

quotes: Zscaler recommends that you deploy Private Service Edges in pairs (N+1), where N is the number of Private Service Edges as per the sizing requirements.
Zscaler recommends that Private Service Edges be deployed in pairs, to ensure continuous availability during software upgrades.

platform-prereqs.statement: A platform needs Intel x86_64/AMD64, systemd, root or sudo, DNS resolution, a provisioning key or OAuth token, and a static MAC address.

quotes: Intel x86_64/AMD64-based architecture
A static MAC address
AMD64-based architecture - systemd
Root or sudo access to the system to configure a new package repository and install packages
DNS resolution and network access

An OAuth 2.0 enrollment token obtained from a hyperscaler marketplace, virtual image, or RPM installer provided by Zscaler, or a Private Service Edge provisioning key obtained from the Zscaler Admin Console

prebuilt-os-updates.statement: Automated OS security updates are available only for prebuilt Private Service Edge images on RHEL 9.x; a Private Service Edge installed manually from an RPM on a custom RHEL 9.x build is not supported.

quotes: Automated OS security updates are only available for prebuilt Private Service Edge images on RHEL 9.x.
Private Service Edges installed manually using an RPM file on a custom RHEL 9.x build are not supported.

org-owns-host-os.statement: Host OS and software-package updates are the organization's responsibility, while Zscaler updates the component software; the captured procedure takes RHEL 9.4 and 9.5 to RHEL 9.6 and later, and Zscaler recommends updating the OS at least every 5 weeks.

quotes: You can use this article to update RHEL 9.4 and 9.5 to RHEL 9.6 and later.
Zscaler recommends updating the OS at least every 5 weeks.
updates to the host operating system (OS) and software packages are the organization's responsibility.
Software components are licensed so that Zscaler can periodically update their software.

os-update-downtime.statement: A host OS update is scheduled by local policy; users should be warned of rolling reconnections, and each component is estimated to be down for 20 minutes.

quotes: The update of the host OS is scheduled according to local policy.
Each software component is estimated to be down for 20 minutes during the update.
Zscaler recommends notifying users of the potential for rolling reconnections during the update window.

groups-for-ha.statement: Zscaler recommends deploying Private Service Edges in groups for high availability and horizontal scaling, and every Private Service Edge belongs to a group.

quotes: Zscaler recommends deploying Private Service Edges for Private Access (ZPA) in groups for high availability and horizontal scaling.
Every Private Service Edge belongs to a specific Private Service Edge group.

active-active.statement: Service Edges are deployed in active-active mode for availability and redundancy.

quotes: They are deployed in active-active mode to ensure availability and redundancy

cpu-headroom.statement: Peak sustained CPU utilization should stay below 70% taking into account all Private Service Edges in the group, so that each stays below 70% if one becomes unavailable; two Private Service Edges both at 50% would exceed 70% on the survivor.

quotes: Peak sustained CPU utilization should be less than 70%.
allow each Private Service Edge to operate under 70% utilization in the event that one of the Private Service Edges becomes unavailable.

For example, if you only have two Private Service Edges and they are both at 50%, this is below the 70% threshold. However, if one Private Service Edge goes down, then the other Private Service Edge runs above 70%.

scale-out-options.statement: To reduce CPU on individual Private Service Edges, add a Private Service Edge to the group, or deploy dedicated groups for specific application segments.

quotes: Deploy an additional Private Service Edge into the Private Service Edge group to distribute users across additional Private Service Edges.
Deploy dedicated Private Service Edge groups for specific application segments

tenant-limits.statement: The ranges and limitations table lists 100 Private Service Edges, 100 Private Service Edge groups and 100 Private Service Edge provisioning keys.

quotes: | Private Service Edges | 100 Private Service Edges |
| Private Service Edge Groups | 100 groups |
| Private Service Edge Provisioning Keys | 100 keys |

quotes: An updated Docker image is available for Private Service Edge for Private Access (ZPA).

evidence.after: Updated Images for App Connector, Private Service Edge, Private Cloud Controller, and Network Connector
quotes: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
Microsoft Azure
Nutanix AHV for App Connector and Private Service Edge
VMware for App Connector, Private Service Edge, and Private Cloud Controller
These image updates include a 4 GB boot partition that exceeds Red Hat's recommendations to help support seamless OS updates.

session-limits.title: Per-instance session limits
session-limits.detail: The prerequisites page gives throughput, CPU, memory and disk sizing but no maximum concurrent sessions or session rate per Private Service Edge. Unverified legacy statement: "Maximum concurrent sessions and session rate per instance." Resolve with Zscaler support.

max-per-group.title: Maximum Private Service Edges per group
max-per-group.detail: The limits table gives a tenant-wide count of 100 (claim tenant-limits) and the prerequisites page gives none per group. Resolve with Zscaler support.

release-images.title: Image and RPM distribution in the 2026 release summary
release-images.detail: The July 23 entries are now sourced (claim images-july23). Unverified legacy statement still open: the August 4 Manager version 26.56.1 provides PSE RPM packages for RHEL 8.x and 9.x from the Zscaler repository; the captured release summary has no August 4 entry. The summary also does not show whether Hyper-V or KVM images exist, the image format on each platform, or Marketplace distribution.

selection-within-group.title: How a session picks a member of a group
selection-within-group.detail: Unverified legacy statement: "The ZPA CA selects among them for each session based on the PSE's health and proximity." The sources say the members are active-active and that new application access moves to other members during an update, but not the selection rule. Resolve with a lab test.
